title: Foot Pain and First MTP Joint Swelling (Gout vs Hallux Rigidus vs Hallux Valgus)
patient_instructions: You are Frank Delgado, a 52-year-old warehouse supervisor. You have had pain and swelling at the base of your right big toe for the past three days. It came on fairly quickly and the joint now feels swollen, red, warm and very tender - even the bedsheet touching it is painful, and it hurts to move the toe or put on a shoe. You have not had any injury or wound. You have NOT had fevers or chills that you have noticed. You enjoy a few beers most nights (4-5 cans) and eat red meat regularly; you had a big seafood barbecue the weekend before this started. You take a fluid tablet (hydrochlorothiazide) for blood pressure. You have had one similar milder attack in the big toe a year ago that settled by itself. No diabetes, not on steroids, no recent travel. IDEAS: you think you may have 'just sprained it' or that it is 'a bit of arthritis'. CONCERNS: you are worried because it is getting worse and you cannot get your boot on for work. EXPECTATIONS: you want to know what it is and to get some pain relief. Affect: uncomfortable, shifting the foot, mildly frustrated. Only volunteer the alcohol, diet, seafood and fluid-tablet details if asked directly; give the previous-attack history if asked about prior episodes.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in an Australian general practice. Frank Delgado, a 52-year-old man, presents with a three-day history of a painful, swollen right big-toe joint. In this 8-minute station: take a focused history (approximately 6 minutes), then you will be shown the following examination findings on screen - the first metatarsophalangeal joint is swollen, red, warm and tender with painful, restricted movement; the patient is afebrile. Using the history and these findings, give the examiner your most likely diagnosis and two or three differentials with reasons, and outline your initial investigations and management. You do not need to perform a physical examination.
examiner_instructions: Reward a structured foot/ankle history (SOCRATES-style pain analysis, pattern, joint screen, trauma, red flags) and, critically, safe reasoning: the candidate must recognise that an acute hot swollen monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise and that a NORMAL temperature does not exclude it. The safe candidate arranges urgent joint aspiration (Gram stain, culture, polarised-light microscopy) before committing to gout - diagnosis of gout requires negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a normal serum urate during a flare does not exclude it. They should elicit the gout risk factors (alcohol, red meat, seafood, thiazide) and identify the thiazide as a precipitant. For management they should cite an eTG-aligned acute option (NSAID e.g. indomethacin/naproxen, OR low-dose colchicine, OR short oral prednisolone) chosen by renal function/comorbidity, with paracetamol as adjunct. Prompt only if stuck: 'Is there anything you must exclude before calling this gout?' Do not give the septic-arthritis point away.

criteria: Structured pain history (site, onset, character, radiation, severity, aggravating/relieving, effect on function) and pattern (night, morning, activity, weight-bearing/limp)
Joint screen (swelling, redness, warmth, deformity, other joints) plus trauma and prior-episode enquiry
Gout risk factors elicited: alcohol, red meat, seafood, sugary drinks and medication (identifies hydrochlorothiazide as a precipitant)
Screens red flags: fever/chills, immunosuppression/diabetes, weight loss, tophi/prior flares
States acute hot swollen monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise and that a normal temperature does not exclude it
Gives gout as most likely with a coherent justification and offers relevant differentials (septic arthritis, hallux rigidus/OA, hallux valgus, pseudogout)
Differentiates hallux rigidus (restricted painful dorsiflexion, dorsal osteophyte) from hallux valgus (deformity, usually painless ROM)
Arranges urgent joint aspiration (MCS + polarised-light microscopy) as the key test before attributing to gout; understands serum urate may be normal in a flare and is deferred
Appropriate investigations: FBE/CRP/ESR, UEC/eGFR (guides NSAID/colchicine dosing), weight-bearing foot X-ray
eTG-aligned acute gout treatment (NSAID OR low-dose colchicine OR short oral prednisolone by renal function/comorbidity; paracetamol adjunct) and reviews the thiazide
Empathic, clear lay explanation of the working diagnosis and plan; addresses the patient's pain and work concerns
Safety-nets and offers appropriate analgesia and follow-up

red_flags: Acute hot, swollen, tender monoarthritis - treat as septic arthritis until joint aspiration excludes it; a normal temperature does NOT rule out septic arthritis
Immunosuppression or diabetes (raises septic-arthritis risk and threshold for urgent aspiration/referral)
Constitutional features (fever, chills, weight loss, night pain) suggesting infection or malignancy/neoplasia in bone
Recent trauma raising possibility of stress or other fracture
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines, Australia) - acute gout: NSAID (e.g. indomethacin or naproxen) OR low-dose colchicine OR a short course of oral prednisolone, selected by comorbidity and renal function; paracetamol as adjunct

eTG - serum urate is frequently normal or low during an acute flare and a normal level does not exclude gout; definitive diagnosis rests on synovial fluid showing negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals
RACGP / Australian practice - an acute hot swollen joint warrants urgent joint aspiration (Gram stain, culture and polarised-light microscopy) to exclude septic arthritis before treatment
PBS - allopurinol for urate-lowering therapy once the flare settles if indicated (recurrent attacks, tophi, urate calculi, CKD), titrated to target serum urate
learning_objectives: Apply a grouped diagnostic-strategy framework to undifferentiated foot pain (probability, serious not-to-be-missed, soft tissue, neurovascular, skin/nail)
Recognise acute monoarthritis as a septic-arthritis emergency and arrange joint aspiration before diagnosing gout
Distinguish gout, hallux rigidus and hallux valgus from history and first-MTP examination findings
Select eTG-aligned acute gout management adjusted for renal function and comorbidity, and review precipitant medications
key_points: Definitive gout diagnosis = negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals on polarised microscopy; diet is a risk factor, not a diagnostic criterion
A normal serum urate during an acute flare does not exclude gout; defer urate testing until the attack settles
Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) raise serum urate and are a recognised gout precipitant - a classic OSCE clue

Hallux rigidus = dorsal osteophyte with painful restricted dorsiflexion (positive grind); hallux valgus = lateral deviation with a medial 'bunion', usually painless ROM - both managed initially with footwear/orthotics and podiatry

citations.claim: Grouped foot/ankle differential (osteoarthritis especially the great toe, plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, ingrowing toenail/paronychia) and 'serious disorders not to be missed' (vascular insufficiency, neoplasia) matches the case's grouped DDx framework.
The case's grouped 'diagnostic strategy model' (probability diagnosis, serious disorders not to be missed) mirrors Murtagh's diagnostic-strategy approach used as the structural template.
Vascular differentials for foot/leg pain (peripheral arterial disease, distinguishing arterial from venous causes) support the case's neurovascular section.
